<reason>The decisive clash was "as designed vs. as adopted." Side B (PRO) argued the motion judges four-day weeks as districts actually run them, that most adopters cut total time, and that savings and learning harm are "the same dial" (the districts saving most are the ones cutting most). Side A (CON) never disputed that most adopters cut time, honestly declined to give a share, and retreated to an existence-proof ("there exists a setting" that saves and harms near zero) that doesn't naturally fit a motion about the policy in aggregate. Worse, A stretched B's concession ("small or near zero" losses for time-holders) across all adopters, and B caught the misattribution cleanly in closing. A's strongest and most original line—retention is itself a learning variable—was real but conceded to be unmeasurable ("noisy"), while B pressed that an unmeasured benefit cannot outweigh a measured loss and that the recruitment edge erodes as neighbors copy. B's equity point (no rural childcare market) also went largely unanswered. Both used A1:/A2: format properly; B was clipped twice, A once, a modest execution cost that does not overturn the substantive edge. A competitive debate, but B made the comparison easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5/B5.1–B5.3: B's "same dial" argument that CON counts savings from time-cutters while disowning their reading scores, combined with catching A's stretching of the "small or near zero" concession from the thin time-holding minority to every adopter, materially damaged A's core "universal help, conditional harm" route.</best_rebuttal>
